question.:question/problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y={x}^{2}$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to point $B(2,4),$ then ${\int }_{C}x\,dx+y\,dy=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j,\,t\in [0,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx+y\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}t\cdot 1+{t}^{2}\cdot 2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}t+2{t}^{3}\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{t}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =[\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{2}^{4}}{2}]-[0] \\  & =2+8 \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y=(x+1)^{2}$ traversed from the point $P(0,1)$ to point $Q(1,4),$ then ${\int }_{C}\frac{dx+dy}{y}=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=(x+1)^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+(t+1)^{2}\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2(t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{dx+dy}{y} & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{y}(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{y}(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1+2(t+1)}{(t+1)^{2}}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{(t+1)^{2}}+\frac{2}{t+1}\,dt \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{t+1}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{1+1}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+1)]-[-\frac{1}{0+1}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1)] \\  & =[-\frac{1}{2}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡2]-[-1+0] \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y={x}^{3}$ traversed from the point $P(1,1)$ to point $Q(2,8),$ then ${\int }_{C}\frac{1}{y}\,dx+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,dy=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{3}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+{t}^{3}\,j,\,t\in [1,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+3{t}^{2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{1}{y}\,dx+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(\frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{t}^{3}}\cdot 1+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\cdot 3{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{t}^{3}}+3\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}}+3t]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{2({2}^{2})}+3(2)]-[-\frac{1}{2({1}^{2})}+3(1)] \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}+6+\frac{1}{2}-3 \\  & =\frac{27}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the curve $y=\sqrt[3]{x}$ traversed from the point $P(0,0)$ to point $Q(1,1),$ then ${\int }_{C}4y{e}^{xy}\,dx+dy=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=\sqrt[3]{x}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j={t}^{3}\,i+t\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=3{t}^{2}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}4y{e}^{xy}\,dx+dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4y{e}^{xy}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(4y{e}^{xy}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4t\cdot {e}^{{t}^{3}\cdot t}\cdot 3{t}^{2}+1\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}12{t}^{3}{e}^{{t}^{4}}+1\,dt \\  & ={[3{e}^{{t}^{4}}+t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[3{e}^{(1)^{4}}+(1)]-[3{e}^{(0)^{4}}+(0)] \\  & =[3e+1]-[3] \\  & =3e-2\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y=\sqrt{x}$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to point $B(1,1),$ then  ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+y)\,dx+(3x+2y)\,dy=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=\sqrt{x}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j={t}^{2}\,i+t\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=2t\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+y)\,dx+(3x+2y)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+(3x+2y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(({x}^{2}+y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(3x+2y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({({t}^{2})}^{2}+t)\cdot 2t+(3{t}^{2}+2t)\cdot 1\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{4}+t)\cdot 2t+3{t}^{2}+2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{t}^{5}+5{t}^{2}+2t\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{6}}{3}+\frac{5{t}^{3}}{3}+{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{(1)^{6}}{3}+\frac{5(1)^{3}}{3}+(1)^{2}]-[0] \\  & =[\frac{1}{3}+\frac{5}{3}+1]-[0] \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y={x}^{2}-x$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to point $B(2,2),$ then ${\int }_{C}2xy\,dx+x\,dy=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{2}-x.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+({t}^{2}-t)\,j,\,t\in [0,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+(2t-1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}2xy\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2xy\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2xy\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2t({t}^{2}-t)\cdot 1+t(2t-1)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2{t}^{3}-t\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{4}}{2}-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =[\frac{{2}^{4}}{2}-\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}]-[0] \\  & =8-2 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y=\pi {x}^{2}$ traversed from the point $A(1,\pi )$ to point $B(2,4\pi ),$ then ${\int }_{C}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{2{x}^{2}})\,dx+3x\,dy=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=\pi {x}^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+\pi {t}^{2}\,j,\,t\in [1,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2\pi t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{2{x}^{2}})\,dx+3x\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{2{x}^{2}})\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+3x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{2{x}^{2}})\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+3x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi {t}^{2}}{2{t}^{2}})\cdot 1+3t\cdot 2\pi t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+6\pi {t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}1+6\pi {t}^{2}\,dt \\  & =[t+2\pi {t}^{3}]_{1}^{2} \\  & =[2+2\pi (2)^{3}]-[1+2\pi (1)^{3}] \\  & =[2+16\pi ]-[1+2\pi ] \\  & =1+14\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y={x}^{2}-1$ traversed from the point $A(0,-1)$ to point $B(2,3),$ then ${\int }_{C}5{x}^{2}y\,dx+{x}^{2}(y+1)\,dy=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{2}-1.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+({t}^{2}-1)\,j,\,t\in [0,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}5{x}^{2}y\,dx+{x}^{2}(y+1)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5{x}^{2}y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+{x}^{2}(y+1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(5{x}^{2}y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+{x}^{2}(y+1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5{t}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\cdot 1+{t}^{2}({t}^{2}-1+1)\cdot 2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5{t}^{4}-5{t}^{2}+2{t}^{5}\,dt \\  & ={[{t}^{5}-\frac{5}{3}{t}^{3}+\frac{{t}^{6}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =[{2}^{5}-\frac{5}{3}(2)^{3}+\frac{{2}^{6}}{3}]-[0] \\  & =32-\frac{40}{3}+\frac{64}{3} \\  & =40\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y={x}^{2}-1$ traversed from the point $P(1,0)$ to point $Q(2,3),$ then ${\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{2}-1.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+({t}^{2}-1)\,j,\,t\in [1,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}({y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{({t}^{2}-1)}^{2}\cdot 1+t\cdot 2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{4}-2{t}^{2}+1+2{t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{4}+1\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}+t]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =[\frac{{2}^{5}}{5}+2]-[\frac{{1}^{5}}{5}+1] \\  & =\frac{32}{5}+2-\frac{1}{5}-1 \\  & =\frac{36}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the curve $y={x}^{3}+1$ traversed from the point $A(0,1)$ to point $B(1,2),$ then ${\int }_{C}x\,dx+(y-1)\,dy=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{3}+1.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+({t}^{3}+1)\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+3{t}^{2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx+(y-1)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+(y-1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(y-1)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t\cdot 1+({t}^{3}+1-1)\cdot 3{t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t+3{t}^{5}\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{t}^{6}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}]-[0] \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y=2 x^{2}$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to point $B(1,2),$ then ${\int }_C\left(2 x\right)\,dx+\left(2 y\right)\,dy=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=2 x^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\left(t\right)\,i+\left(2 t^{2}\right)\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)&=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=\left(1\right)\,i+\left(4 t\right)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_C\left(2 x\right)\,dx+\left(2 y\right)\,dy &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(2 x\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\left(2 y\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(\left(2 x\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\left(2 y\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(2 \left(t\right)\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(2 \left(2 t^{2}\right)\right)\cdot \left(4 t\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}2 t+16 t^{3}\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}16 t^{3} + 2 t\,dt \\  &=\left[t^{2}+4 t^{4}\right]_{0}^{1} \\  &=[\left(1\right)^{2}+4 \left(1\right)^{4}]-[\left(0\right)^{2}+4 \left(0\right)^{4}] \\  &=[1+4]-[0+0] \\  &=5\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y=3 x^{2}$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to point $B(1,3),$ then ${\int }_C\left(y\right)\,dx+\left(3 x\right)\,dy=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=3 x^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\left(t\right)\,i+\left(3 t^{2}\right)\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)&=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=\left(1\right)\,i+\left(6 t\right)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_C\left(y\right)\,dx+\left(3 x\right)\,dy &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(y\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\left(3 x\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(\left(y\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\left(3 x\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(\left(3 t^{2}\right)\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(3 \left(t\right)\right)\cdot \left(6 t\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}3 t^{2}+18 t^{2}\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}21 t^{2}\,dt \\  &=\left[7 t^{3}\right]_{0}^{1} \\  &=[7 \left(1\right)^{3}]-[7 \left(0\right)^{3}] \\  &=[7]-[0] \\  &=7\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y=3 \pi x^{2}$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to point $B(2,12 \pi),$ then ${\int }_C\left(\cos{\left(\frac{y}{x^{2}} \right)}\right)\,dx+\left(x^{2}\right)\,dy=$ The composed integrand at the initial endpoint is interpreted by its one-sided continuous extension along $C.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=3 \pi x^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\left(t\right)\,i+\left(3 \pi t^{2}\right)\,j,\,t\in [0,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)&=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=\left(1\right)\,i+\left(6 \pi t\right)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_C\left(\cos{\left(\frac{y}{x^{2}} \right)}\right)\,dx+\left(x^{2}\right)\,dy &={\int }_{0}^{2}\left(\cos{\left(\frac{y}{x^{2}} \right)}\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\left(x^{2}\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  &={\int }_{0}^{2}\left(\left(\cos{\left(\frac{y}{x^{2}} \right)}\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\left(x^{2}\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{2}\left(\cos{\left(\frac{\left(3 \pi t^{2}\right)}{\left(t\right)^{2}} \right)}\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(\left(t\right)^{2}\right)\cdot \left(6 \pi t\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{2}-1+6 \pi t^{3}\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{2}6 \pi t^{3} - 1\,dt \\  &=\left[- t+\frac{3 \pi t^{4}}{2}\right]_{0}^{2} \\  &=[- \left(2\right)+\frac{3 \pi \left(2\right)^{4}}{2}]-[- \left(0\right)+\frac{3 \pi \left(0\right)^{4}}{2}] \\  &=[-2+24 \pi]-[0+0] \\  &=-2 + 24 \pi\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y=x^{2}$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to point $B(1,1),$ then ${\int }_C\left(3 y\right)\,dx+\left(2 x\right)\,dy=$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)&=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=\left(1\right)\,i+\left(2 t\right)\,j.\end{aligned}

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_C\left(3 y\right)\,dx+\left(2 x\right)\,dy &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(3 y\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\left(2 x\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(\left(3 y\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\left(2 x\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(3 \left(t^{2}\right)\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(2 \left(t\right)\right)\cdot \left(2 t\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}3 t^{2}+4 t^{2}\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}7 t^{2}\,dt \\  &=\left[\frac{7 t^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{1} \\  &=[\frac{7 \left(1\right)^{3}}{3}]-[\frac{7 \left(0\right)^{3}}{3}] \\  &=[\frac{7}{3}]-[0] \\  &=\frac{7}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y=x^{2} - 3$ traversed from the point $A(0,-3)$ to point $B(2,1),$ then ${\int }_C\left(x^{2} y\right)\,dx+\left(3 x^{2} \left(y + 3\right)\right)\,dy=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=x^{2} - 3.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\left(t\right)\,i+\left(t^{2} - 3\right)\,j,\,t\in [0,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)&=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=\left(1\right)\,i+\left(2 t\right)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_C\left(x^{2} y\right)\,dx+\left(3 x^{2} \left(y + 3\right)\right)\,dy &={\int }_{0}^{2}\left(x^{2} y\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\left(3 x^{2} \left(y + 3\right)\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  &={\int }_{0}^{2}\left(\left(x^{2} y\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\left(3 x^{2} \left(y + 3\right)\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{2}\left(\left(t\right)^{2} \left(t^{2} - 3\right)\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(3 \left(t\right)^{2} \left(\left(t^{2} - 3\right) + 3\right)\right)\cdot \left(2 t\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{2}t^{4} - 3 t^{2}+6 t^{5}\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{2}6 t^{5} + t^{4} - 3 t^{2}\,dt \\  &=\left[\frac{t^{5}}{5}- t^{3}+t^{6}\right]_{0}^{2} \\  &=[\frac{\left(2\right)^{5}}{5}- \left(2\right)^{3}+\left(2\right)^{6}]-[\frac{\left(0\right)^{5}}{5}- \left(0\right)^{3}+\left(0\right)^{6}] \\  &=[\frac{32}{5}-8+64]-[0+0+0] \\  &=\frac{312}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y=3 x^{2}$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to point $B(1,3),$ then ${\int }_C\left(x\right)\,dx+\left(3 y\right)\,dy=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=3 x^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\left(t\right)\,i+\left(3 t^{2}\right)\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)&=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=\left(1\right)\,i+\left(6 t\right)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_C\left(x\right)\,dx+\left(3 y\right)\,dy &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(x\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\left(3 y\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(\left(x\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\left(3 y\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(\left(t\right)\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(3 \left(3 t^{2}\right)\right)\cdot \left(6 t\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}t+54 t^{3}\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}54 t^{3} + t\,dt \\  &=\left[\frac{t^{2}}{2}+\frac{27 t^{4}}{2}\right]_{0}^{1} \\  &=[\frac{\left(1\right)^{2}}{2}+\frac{27 \left(1\right)^{4}}{2}]-[\frac{\left(0\right)^{2}}{2}+\frac{27 \left(0\right)^{4}}{2}] \\  &=[\frac{1}{2}+\frac{27}{2}]-[0+0] \\  &=14\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y=x^{2}$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to point $B(1,1),$ then ${\int }_C\left(3 x\right)\,dx+\left(2 y\right)\,dy=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=x^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\left(t\right)\,i+\left(t^{2}\right)\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)&=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=\left(1\right)\,i+\left(2 t\right)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_C\left(3 x\right)\,dx+\left(2 y\right)\,dy &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(3 x\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\left(2 y\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(\left(3 x\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\left(2 y\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(3 \left(t\right)\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(2 \left(t^{2}\right)\right)\cdot \left(2 t\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}3 t+4 t^{3}\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}4 t^{3} + 3 t\,dt \\  &=\left[\frac{3 t^{2}}{2}+t^{4}\right]_{0}^{1} \\  &=[\frac{3 \left(1\right)^{2}}{2}+\left(1\right)^{4}]-[\frac{3 \left(0\right)^{2}}{2}+\left(0\right)^{4}] \\  &=[\frac{3}{2}+1]-[0+0] \\  &=\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y=3 \pi x^{2}$ traversed from the point $A(1,3 \pi)$ to point $B(3,27 \pi),$ then ${\int }_C\left(\sin{\left(\frac{y}{2 x^{2}} \right)}\right)\,dx+\left(x\right)\,dy=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=3 \pi x^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\left(t\right)\,i+\left(3 \pi t^{2}\right)\,j,\,t\in [1,3]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)&=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=\left(1\right)\,i+\left(6 \pi t\right)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_C\left(\sin{\left(\frac{y}{2 x^{2}} \right)}\right)\,dx+\left(x\right)\,dy &={\int }_{1}^{3}\left(\sin{\left(\frac{y}{2 x^{2}} \right)}\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\left(x\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  &={\int }_{1}^{3}\left(\left(\sin{\left(\frac{y}{2 x^{2}} \right)}\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\left(x\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{1}^{3}\left(\sin{\left(\frac{\left(3 \pi t^{2}\right)}{2 \left(t\right)^{2}} \right)}\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(\left(t\right)\right)\cdot \left(6 \pi t\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{1}^{3}-1+6 \pi t^{2}\,dt \\  &={\int }_{1}^{3}6 \pi t^{2} - 1\,dt \\  &=\left[- t+2 \pi t^{3}\right]_{1}^{3} \\  &=[- \left(3\right)+2 \pi \left(3\right)^{3}]-[- \left(1\right)+2 \pi \left(1\right)^{3}] \\  &=[-3+54 \pi]-[-1+2 \pi] \\  &=-2 + 52 \pi\end{aligned}
$$
